recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order, and say which formula you reach for and why.

steps.label: State the double-angle formula
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the book prints [1 Mark] for writing the formula alone. 2Tan⁻¹x has three standard conversions; the Cos⁻¹ one is chosen because the other term is a Sin⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: 2Tan⁻¹x = Cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)). The Cos⁻¹ form is chosen because the other term is a Sin⁻¹.

recall.must_convey: That the conversion 2Tan⁻¹x = Cos⁻¹((1−x²)/(1+x²)) is stated.

steps.why: 2Tan⁻¹x can be written as a Sin⁻¹, a Cos⁻¹ or a Tan⁻¹. The Cos⁻¹ form is chosen because it matches the Sin⁻¹(4/5) already on the page and closes in one line with Sin⁻¹x + Cos⁻¹x = π/2. The Sin⁻¹ and Tan⁻¹ forms also reach π/2, but each needs one more identity.
common_mistakes: Pairing the wrong argument with the wrong inverse: (1 − x²)/(1 + x²) goes with Cos⁻¹, while 2x/(1 + x²) is the Sin⁻¹ form.

steps.label: Substitute x = 1/3
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Substitute and simplify the compound fraction: (1 − 1/9) over (1 + 1/9) is (8/9) over (10/9).
steps.memory_tip: (1/3)² is 1/9, not 1/6. The fraction becomes (8/9) over (10/9).

recall.must_convey: That x = 1/3 is substituted, giving Cos⁻¹((1 − 1/9)/(1 + 1/9)).

steps.why: Squaring 1/3 gives 1/9, not 1/6. That single arithmetic step decides everything after it.
common_mistakes: Substituting into the wrong part of the fraction.

steps.label: Simplify to Cos⁻¹(4/5)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The ninths cancel: (8/9) ÷ (10/9) is 8/10, which reduces to 4/5. That 4/5 matching the other term is the whole design of the question.
steps.memory_tip: The ninths cancel: 8/10 reduces to 4/5, matching the other term — that is the design of the question.

recall.must_convey: That the compound fraction simplifies to 8/10 = 4/5, so 2Tan⁻¹(1/3) = Cos⁻¹(4/5).

steps.why: The 4/5 is not a coincidence — the question was built so that the converted term matches the Sin⁻¹(4/5) already present. That match is what makes the last line work.

steps.label: Apply Sin⁻¹x + Cos⁻¹x = π/2
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Both terms are now inverses of the SAME value, 4/5 — and Sin⁻¹x + Cos⁻¹x is always π/2, whatever x is.

common_mistakes: Applying the identity when the two arguments differ.

insider_note: Convert 2Tan⁻¹(1/3) into Cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) = Cos⁻¹(4/5), which is chosen to match the 4/5 already present. Then Sin⁻¹x + Cos⁻¹x = π/2 finishes it in a single line.
